HKJA|記協

Related: 📰 Press Freedom under Siege | FCC | Stand News | The Witness

The Hong Kong Journalists Association (香港記者協會, "記協"; HKJA) is the city's principal trade union for working journalists. Founded in 1968, it is an affiliate of the International Federation of Journalists (IFJ) and a member of the global free-expression network IFEX, and for more than half a century it was the main independent voice defending Hong Kong's press — its stated purpose being "to enhance press freedom and the integrity of news coverage" and to improve journalists' working conditions.

Through the decades the HKJA became the institution that measured the freedom it defended. It ran an annual Press Freedom Index survey of journalists and the public, co-organised the regional Human Rights Press Awards (with the Foreign Correspondents' Club and Amnesty International), published yearly reports on the state of the media, and provided legal and practical support to reporters facing arrest, assault or intimidation while covering the news.

A union under siege

Since the 2019 protests and the 2020 National Security Law, the HKJA has itself become a target of the crackdown it documents — part of the wider story told on the Press Freedom under Siege hub.

  • A shrinking membership. As the newsrooms that employed its members were shut down — Apple Daily, Stand News, Citizen News — and journalists left the profession or the city, membership and finances collapsed. By June 2024 the association reported just 338 members, and successive chairs have warned of severe financial strain.
  • Smears and official pressure. State-affiliated media and senior officials have repeatedly attacked the group, questioning its legitimacy and representativeness. In June 2024 the Security Bureau publicly admonished newly elected committee members, and two nominees withdrew.
  • The Human Rights Press Awards, abandoned. The awards the HKJA had co-run for decades were effectively ended in 2022 after the FCC pulled out, citing legal risk under the security law.

Its chairs, prosecuted and pressured

The people who have led the HKJA trace the pressure on the whole profession:

  • Ronson Chan (陳朗昇), chair 2021–2024 and a former deputy assignment editor at Stand News, was arrested in September 2022 while reporting on a homeowners' meeting in Mong Kok and charged with obstructing a police officer who had demanded his ID. Convicted in 2023 and sentenced to 5 days in jail, he lost his appeal on 29 May 2026 and was jailed immediately, later taking the case to the Court of Final Appeal. RSF called his imprisonment "a new low for press freedom in Hong Kong." He had declined to seek re-election in 2024, saying the combined attacks on him and the HKJA had grown too damaging.
  • Selina Cheng (鄭嘉如), a Wall Street Journal reporter, was elected chair in July 2024 — and fired by the WSJ days later, having said her employer pressured her not to stand. She has led the association since.

The HKJA continues to issue statements defending reporters — in October 2026 insisting that "reporting is not sedition" after an online journalist's arrest (see Press Freedom under Siege) — even as its own survival is in question.

noteIndex.title: SHKO(Save Hong Kong Online)
noteIndex.body:
[![Great Extinction](/assets/extinctions.jpeg)](/notes/wx39zljncctue32jn06u29u/) 
> (_Courtesy: [Hong Kong Freepress](https://hongkongfp.com/2021/11/28/explainer-over-50-groups-gone-in-11-months-how-hong-kongs-pro-democracy-forces-crumbled/), 2021_) 

SHKO (Save Hong Kong Online) is a community-driven project dedicated to preserving the rapidly disappearing websites and online resources of Hong Kong’s civil society and independent media since 2019. In response to the sweeping shutdowns caused by political changes in Hong Kong, we aim to safeguard digital heritage before it vanishes. This project is anonymous, open source, and supported by a global network of contributors.

While most sites in our archive were forced offline due to Hong Kong’s political deterioration, it’s important to note that [[RFA Cantonese|sites.rfa_cantonese]] is the only site here closed not because of Hong Kong’s situation, but due to internal political decisions in the United States.

Explore our full list of preserved sites and archives on the [Collections page](/notes/wx39zljncctue32jn06u29u/).

Recent work: documenting the [[Hong Kong Fire 2025|hong-kong-fire-2025]] tragedy at Wang Fuk Court (168 dead, ongoing probes into flammable mesh/foam, bid-rigging, and a judge-led review), including activism, timeline, and investigation subpages; and the [[⚖️ Jimmy Lai case|faces-of-the-crackdown.jimmy-lai]] — Apple Daily founder sentenced to 20 years under the National Security Law (Feb 2026), with coverage of press freedom impact and international response; and [[🎵 Glory to Hong Kong|glory-to-hong-kong]] — the 2019 protest anthem and the 2024 court order that made it the first song banned in Hong Kong since the 1997 handover; and [[📕 Book Censorship under the NSL|book-censorship]] — how Hong Kong criminalised the printed word, from the banned Sheep Village children's-book trilogy (whose speech-therapist authors were jailed for sedition) and purged public libraries to the 2026 bookshop raids; and [[🗽 Statues & Monuments|statues]] — how Hong Kong's public monuments to Tiananmen and the 2019 protests (the Pillar of Shame, the Goddess of Democracy, Lady Liberty) were removed, seized as police evidence, and driven into exile abroad; and [[⚖️ The Hong Kong 47|hong-kong-47]] — the largest National Security Law case, in which 45 pro-democracy figures were jailed for up to 10 years over a 2020 opposition primary election; and [[🕯️ Tiananmen Vigil|tiananmen-vigil]] — the thirty-year Victoria Park candlelight vigil for the 1989 crackdown, the largest June 4th commemoration on Chinese soil, now banned and its organisers jailed; and [[✊ Faces of the Crackdown|faces-of-the-crackdown]] — a human index to the publishers, students, unionists and clergy jailed, exiled or tried under the National Security Law; and [[🎬 Films & Documentaries|films]] — the protest movement on film, a decade of documentaries and features (Ten Years, Revolution of Our Times, the Joshua Wong doc) now largely banned or unshowable in Hong Kong, gathered with their trailers; and [[📰 Press Freedom under Siege|press-freedom]] — how one of Asia's freest presses was dismantled in five years, from the raids that closed Apple Daily and Stand News to the revived sedition law now reaching lone online reporters.

## Goals
- To preserve as much information as possible before its disappearance during Hong Kong's great transition
- To illustrate a viable method that everyone can use to help preserve online heritage with no pains
- To demonstrate global collaborations to save local digital heritages with best practices

## Quick Facts

We are working on over dozens of [[websites or online causes | sites]] in Hong Kong in the past two decades which has been forced to shutdown or at the brink of disappearing. We'd welcome anyone help [[contribute | participation]] to the content and/or [[sponsor | sponsorship]] our program to sustain it together. 

Examples:
- [[sites.appledaily]] (Extincted)
- [[sites.inmediahk]] (In Danger)
